claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen introduces local disorder into HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach couples defect-aware first-principles DFT with atomistic models of phonon and electronic scattering.
The proposed approach will independently and quantitatively predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The method will reduce prediction error by 20–30% relative to Debye-temperature-based analytical models.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Between 300 and 1200 K, experimental total thermal conductivity of oxygen-bearing HfNbTaTiZr lies between 10 and 17 W/(K·m).
Defects and impurities induce local disorder and variations in interatomic force constants.
Defect-induced local disorder and force-constant variations alter both phonon and electron scattering.
Explicit atomistic treatment can avoid oversimplifications associated with unified analytical estimates.
Separating phonon and electron scattering will improve thermal-transport accuracy for both pristine and impurity-bearing HfNbTaTiZr.
At temperatures below 200 K, each predicted transport contribution will agree with its corresponding experimental value within ±25%.
The predicted low-temperature lattice and electronic contributions will have similar magnitudes.
Between 300 and 1200 K, the predicted total conductivity will fall within 10–17 W/(K·m).
Earlier approaches varied atomic masses or force constants, used Debye approximations, or combined DFT-derived elastic properties with analytical conductivity estimates.
Earlier approaches assumed perfect, defect-free crystals.
Earlier approaches conflated lattice and electronic heat-transport mechanisms.
The proposed model is applicable below 200 K for separate-channel comparisons and from 300 to 1200 K for total-conductivity comparisons.
The model may not extend to temperatures outside the stated ranges or to impurity concentrations substantially different from approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Sample preparation and measurement variability may affect model-to-experiment comparisons.
